title: 355: The Giant Pool of Money
why: Made the subprime mortgage meltdown understandable to a mass audience, won a Peabody, and directly led to the creation of Planet Money.

title: 310: Habeas Schmabeas
why: A Peabody-winning examination of Guantanamo detainees and the erosion of habeas corpus at the height of the war on terror.

title: 296: After the Flood
why: Captured the human aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and is regularly ranked among the show's best hours.

title: 360: Switched at Birth
why: The story of two families who learn decades later that their daughters were swapped in the hospital became one of the show's most beloved and recommended episodes, and an Ira Glass personal favorite.

title: 403: NUMMI
why: Its account of the GM-Toyota joint venture plant became a widely circulated case study on corporate culture and lean manufacturing.

title: 405: Inside Job
why: Its reporting with ProPublica on the hedge fund Magnetar's role in the housing bubble was part of coverage that won a Pulitzer Prize.

title: 414: Right to Remain Silent
why: Aired secret recordings made by NYPD officer Adrian Schoolcraft that exposed arrest and summons quotas inside his precinct.

title: 430: Very Tough Love
why: Its investigation of a Georgia drug court judge won a Polk Award and set off a public dispute and official scrutiny.

title: 441: When Patents Attack!
why: Made the patent troll problem a mainstream tech-policy topic and drew heavy debate, including formal responses from the companies involved.

title: 454: Mr. Daisey and the Apple Factory
why: Mike Daisey's monologue about Foxconn working conditions became the show's most downloaded episode before key parts were found to be fabricated.

title: 460: Retraction
why: The show devoted a full hour to retracting the Daisey story, which set a listening record and became a landmark moment in journalism ethics.

title: 465: What Happened at Dos Erres
why: Its reporting with ProPublica on a Guatemalan massacre survivor raised by one of the soldiers won a Peabody Award.

title: 487: Harper High School, Part One
why: Producers spent five months inside a Chicago school scarred by gun violence, and the two-part series won a Peabody.

title: 490: Trends With Benefits
why: Its investigation of the surge in federal disability claims sparked fierce national debate and pushback from critics and policy experts.

title: Episode 67 - Robin Williams
why: Williams spoke candidly about addiction and suicidal thoughts, the episode took on new weight after his death, and it was added to the Library of Congress National Recording Registry.

title: Episode 75 - Carlos Mencia
why: Maron confronted Mencia about the joke-theft accusations that had dogged him, producing a rare unguarded moment that the comedy world talked about for weeks.

title: Episode 111 - Louis CK part 1
why: Two estranged friends worked through an old rift on mic, and Slate later ranked the two-parter the greatest podcast episode ever made.

title: Episode 145 - Gallagher
why: The prop comic stormed out mid-interview when Maron pressed him on bigoted material, producing one of the show's most infamous moments.

title: Episode 245 - Todd Glass
why: Comedian Todd Glass came out as gay publicly for the first time, making headlines and showing the show could host major personal revelations.

title: Space
why: An early episode that fused science with emotion, anchored by Ann Druyan's account of the Voyager Golden Record and her romance with Carl Sagan, and it appears on several all-time lists.

title: Words
why: Its story of a deaf man who reached adulthood without any language became one of the show's most shared explorations of how words shape thought.

title: Patient Zero
why: It traced the origins of outbreaks such as HIV and typhoid back to their first cases and became a frequently recommended entry point to the show.

title: Colors
why: Its exploration of why ancient texts barely mention the color blue spread widely online and lands on all-time best-episode lists.

title: Yellow Rain
why: Robert Krulwich's aggressive interview with a Hmong refugee and author provoked a major backlash over race and power in journalism, followed by a public apology.

title: 15: Sounds of the Artificial World
why: Its look at the designers behind everyday digital sounds became a signature episode and landed on Slate's list of the best podcast episodes ever.

title: 66: Kowloon Walled City
why: Its portrait of Hong Kong's lawless, ultra-dense enclave became one of the show's most cited episodes as it grew into a design-podcast phenomenon.

title: Episode 27: Ghosts of the Ostfront I
why: This opener of Carlin's vivid series on the Nazi-Soviet war defined the show's marathon style, and Slate ranked it among the all-time best podcast episodes.

title: Episode 39: Death Throes of the Republic VI
why: The roughly five-and-a-half-hour finale of Carlin's fall-of-Rome series showed podcasts could sustain epic, audiobook-length history, and the AV Club named the series a defining podcast moment.

title: Episode 48: Prophets of Doom
why: Its account of the apocalyptic Münster Rebellion is a standout standalone episode that appears on all-time best-episode lists.

title: Episode 50: Blueprint for Armageddon I
why: This launched Carlin's World War I series, which became his most famous work and a gateway into history podcasting for millions of listeners.

title: 179 - The End
why: The finale of Mike Duncan's award-winning five-year chronicle capped the series that inspired a whole wave of narrative history podcasts.

title: We Bought A Toxic Asset!
why: The team pooled their own money to buy a slice of a mortgage bond and track its decline, a stunt that defined the show's hands-on approach to explanation.

title: 150: Time Bobby
why: Bobby Moynihan's time-traveling character sparked a running improvised saga, and both Slate and the AV Club cite the episode as a high point of podcast comedy.

title: Series 1, Episode 7
why: It captured the Gervais-Merchant-Pilkington dynamic on a show Guinness certified as the most downloaded podcast, which introduced countless listeners to podcasting.

title: 1 - Pilot
why: The debut of the surreal community-radio fiction built a fully formed world from the start, then went viral on Tumblr and topped the iTunes charts in 2013.

title: Origin Stories
why: Nate DiMeo turned his miniature-history form toward his own family archive, and Slate named it one of the best podcast episodes ever.

title: Bayard Rustin: Who Is This Man?
why: It brought overdue attention to the openly gay civil-rights strategist behind the March on Washington and appears on Slate's all-time list.

title: Strange Fruit: Voices of a Lynching
why: Witness testimony and archival tape revealed the 1930 Indiana lynching behind the famous song, and Slate ranked it third among all podcast episodes.

title: Franny's Last Ride
why: Comedian Mike DeStefano's story of a final motorcycle ride with his dying wife is among the most celebrated stories The Moth has ever shared.

title: Secrets
why: This early experiment in intimate audio storytelling, including a look at the PostSecret project, helped pioneer the independent narrative podcast.

title: Episode 109
why: Recorded right after California's Proposition 8 passed, it channeled outrage and community into a show Slate ranked among the best podcast episodes.

title: Don't Leave Me This Way
why: It wove together three stories about one song's power through loss, illness, and faith, and earned a place on Slate's all-time list.

show: The Best Show on WFMU with Tom Scharpling
title: Dec. 14, 2010
why: An unhinged holiday call-in show that fans and Slate hold up as the cult program at its most chaotic.

title: Walt Whitman, Featuring James Adomian
why: James Adomian's sustained, exuberant improvised Walt Whitman made this a standout of literary comedy podcasting.

title: Tango & Cash
why: The bad-movie hosts at their most gleeful, discussing a film they genuinely love, in an episode Slate named among the best ever.

title: Episode 300
why: The long-running film show marked its milestone by ranking the decade's best movies, a two-part episode that became a touchstone for movie podcasting.

show: The B.S. Report with Bill Simmons
title: B.S. Report: Barack Obama
why: A sitting president sat down for a sports podcast and riffed on Jeremy Lin and college football playoffs, generating national headlines.

title: SModcast 259: The Walrus and the Carpenter
why: Kevin Smith and Scott Mosier's riff on a bizarre walrus-costume ad became the feature film Tusk, a rare case of a podcast bit turning into a Hollywood movie.

title: This Pig Wants To Party: Maurice Sendak's Latest
why: An aging Sendak's tender, tearful reflections on mortality moved listeners so deeply that the interview was later animated by Christoph Niemann and widely shared.
